meta.title: E-Waste & Carbon Accounting in IT
meta.subtitle: Executive edition — a self-study companion. Everything you need to work through the day is on this page; no mentor required.
meta.levelNote: a management topic: governance, procurement, compliance, reporting and investment decisions, not just operational sustainability.
meta.howToUse: Lectures happen away from the screen. Use this page during the independent work blocks — read the short brief, run the mechanic once, look at the result. One loop takes minutes, not tens of minutes.
meta.footerLine: AION Green IT · Module 2 · Day 3 · English (executive edition)

opening.scene: Monday, 09:14. Your largest client's procurement lead wants two things attached to this quarter's re-tender: your IT carbon figures, and proof that retired devices are handled responsibly. Your team has neither the numbers nor the paper trail — and the deadline is Friday.
opening.turn: No slogan fixes this. Today builds the two things that do: numbers you can defend, and decisions that hold up. Work the four blocks below — each one hands you part of the answer.

stakes.label: The deal
stakes.text: Tenders and key accounts now ask for IT carbon and disposal proof. “We don't track that” can lose the contract.

stakes.label: The law
stakes.text: Reporting duties and data-protection rules follow every device that leaves the building, documented or not.

stakes.label: The budget
stakes.text: Replacing devices early and losing their resale value quietly burns money that lifecycle thinking would keep.

stakes.label: The reputation
stakes.text: A visible but hollow “green” move is exposed the moment anyone audits it — worse than doing nothing.

sections.title: The basics, in one pass
sections.intro: Two intertwined control topics across the IT lifecycle: e-waste and carbon accounting. Each card shows a diagram and how its parts connect; open it for the analogy, a concrete example, and what you actually use it for.

concepts.title: What e-waste is — and why it's a management issue
concepts.relation: One retired device is tied to four management concerns at once — so it belongs on the management desk, not only the facilities one.
points: Retired IT hardware: laptops, phones, servers, network gear and their parts.
It ties up capital, carries compliance and data-security duties, and customers now ask about it.
concepts.analogy: It's not scrap in a cupboard — it's an unmanaged asset, like a company car nobody logged the sale of.
concepts.example: A 3-year-old laptop still holds resale value, reuse potential and — until it's wiped and tracked — live company data and a legal duty.
concepts.useFor: Use this framing to lift e-waste off the facilities budget line and onto the management agenda: it's capital, compliance and reputation, not just disposal.

concepts.title: Where e-waste actually comes from
concepts.relation: The four causes all act upstream — at buying and replacing — long before anything reaches the bin downstream.
points: Short, fixed replacement cycles; no repair path; little reuse.
Unstructured returns — devices leave with no clear record.
concepts.analogy: The bin fills at the checkout, not at the recycling plant: like buying bottled water by the pallet, the waste is decided when you purchase.
concepts.example: A fixed 3-year swap retires 650 laptops that mostly still work — that waste was scheduled at procurement, years before disposal.
concepts.useFor: Use it to aim at the real lever: change replacement rules and procurement criteria, not just the disposal contract at the end.

concepts.title: The disposal ladder — five different things
concepts.relation: Each rung down keeps less of the effort already spent building the device — so the rungs are ranked, not interchangeable.
points: Disposal → recycling → remanufacturing → refurbishment → reuse, with prevention at the top.
Reuse and refurbishment keep the embodied (“grey”) energy; recycling loses most of it.
concepts.analogy: Like clothes: mend and re-wear beats donating, which beats shredding for rags. Every step down loses more of the original work.
concepts.example: Refurbishing a laptop keeps the energy already spent making it; recycling recovers some metal but throws that build-energy away.
concepts.useFor: Use the ladder to challenge “we recycle” as a finish line — reuse and refurbishment sit higher and cut more carbon per device.

concepts.title: Carbon accounting — how Scopes 1, 2 and 3 connect
concepts.relation: The scopes don't overlap — they nest around your company boundary and add up to one total. One firm's Scope 1 is another's Scope 3: your cloud provider's electricity (their Scope 2) lands in your Scope 3.
points: Scope 1: direct, on-site emissions you own. Scope 2: the energy you buy.
Scope 3: everything up- and downstream — making devices, cloud, disposal. For IT, usually the biggest slice.
concepts.analogy: Think of a household: Scope 1 is your car's exhaust, Scope 2 is your electricity bill, Scope 3 is everything you buy — the factory, the shipping, the landfill.
concepts.example: For one laptop: Scope 1 ≈ nothing on-site; Scope 2 = the power it draws at your desk; Scope 3 = the Asian factory, the freight, the cloud it talks to, and its disposal.
concepts.useFor: Use scopes to aim: for IT most emissions hide in Scope 3, so counting only 1 and 2 makes you look clean while missing most of the footprint.

concepts.title: IT's CO₂ hotspots across the lifecycle
concepts.relation: Carbon is spread around the whole loop, not at one point — and recycling feeds materials back to the start, closing it.
points: Hotspots: production, transport, daily operation, cloud, user devices, data centres, disposal.
Each depends on databases, emission factors and where you draw the system boundary.
concepts.analogy: Like a flight's footprint: it's not just fuel in the air (use), but building the plane (manufacture) and running the airport (data centre, cloud).
concepts.example: A phone can emit most of its lifetime CO₂ before you unbox it — in manufacturing — while a server emits most of its own during years of operation.
concepts.useFor: Use the map to match the fix to the device: extend life where manufacturing dominates, improve efficiency where operation dominates.

concepts.title: Measuring is not the point — steering is
concepts.relation: Data only matters once it feeds a decision; a number with no decision attached is a report on a shelf.
points: Carbon accounting exists to enable decisions, not to produce a report for its own sake.
There's a real trade-off between accuracy, practicality, data availability and management need.
concepts.analogy: A bathroom scale doesn't make you fitter — the decisions you take because of the number do.
concepts.example: A rough but timely baseline (“cloud is ~40% of our IT emissions”) lets you act this quarter; a perfect figure that lands next year decides nothing.
concepts.useFor: Use carbon data to decide, and accept the trade-off between accuracy, effort and speed — a usable estimate beats a perfect number that's too late.

map.title: The one picture to remember
map.caption: E-waste and carbon accounting are the same story seen twice: both run the length of the device lifecycle, and both roll up into how the company is governed and reported. Steer them together, not apart.

sections.title: Where is Nexora weakest? — Nexora Digital Services
sections.intro: You are the IT-governance lead / sustainability consultant for Nexora Digital Services: growing internationally, large device volumes, hybrid IT, mounting pressure to make the old-device inventory and CO₂ impact traceable — with no consistent steering model yet. Before you can propose anything, you need to know where it actually hurts. Sort every signal into Source, Cycle or Control — some are the real weak spot, others just look alarming. Name the one area you'd bring into the room, because that call carries into the work ahead.
sections.doneRule: Sort every signal, then name the weak spot.
sections.resetNote: Clears your sorting and your diagnosis — the rest of the page stays as it is.
sections.areasRelation: The three areas are one device's life in order: what you buy (Source) → how it runs (Cycle) → whether you can see it and close it out (Control). A risk in any one is a management gap in that phase.

categories.name: Source
categories.blurb: Procurement & replacement — the decisions that create devices in the first place.

categories.name: Cycle
categories.blurb: Use & operations — what happens while the device is in service.

categories.name: Control
categories.blurb: Data, transparency & disposal — whether you can see and steer it.

clues.text: Each country office buys its own devices locally instead of going through one central contract.
clues.explain: Sounds risky, but every region already applies the same repairability- and energy-rating checklist before purchase — buying locally hasn't lowered device quality or shortened lifespans.
clues.why: Decentralised isn't automatically unmanaged — check the criteria before you judge the shape of the process.

clues.text: No one at Nexora can currently produce a single number for how many devices are active across its country offices.
clues.explain: This is the real gap: with no shared device inventory, there is no baseline to report from anywhere in the lifecycle.
clues.why: You can't defend a carbon figure for hardware you can't even count.

clues.text: Staff keep the same laptop through the full replacement cycle even as they move between office and home.
clues.explain: Reads like neglect, but Nexora already runs an annual health-check that reassigns or upgrades machines that no longer fit the workload — the review just isn't visible from outside IT.
clues.why: An in-service device that still fits the job isn't a red flag by itself.

clues.text: Retired laptops from three regional offices sit in local storage rooms with no shared record of quantity, condition or next destination.
clues.explain: Missing chain-of-custody across regions is exactly the transparency gap a customer audit will not accept.
clues.why: “Somewhere in a cupboard, we think” does not survive a tender review.

clues.text: Nexora's device replacement cycle varies by country, from two to four years.
clues.explain: A varying cycle looks inconsistent, but each region sets its own cycle against local usage data — a deliberate, reviewed choice, not drift.
clues.why: A different number isn't automatically a worse number — ask what it's based on.

clues.text: Energy-saving settings differ from laptop to laptop across the fleet.
clues.explain: Inconsistent settings sound like waste, but the difference traces to role-based power profiles IT already manages — not to nobody looking at operational energy.
clues.why: Variation is only a problem if no one chose it on purpose.

clues.text: IT has never been asked to report a CO₂ figure for hardware, so no one currently owns producing one.
clues.explain: No owner, no baseline, no agreed system boundary — the transparency the client is pushing for doesn't exist yet.
clues.why: A rough baseline you can defend beats a precise one you don't have.

diagnosis.prompt: You've read every signal. If you had to name ONE weak spot to bring into the room, which is it?
diagnosis.correctVerdict: Control. The device count, its whereabouts and its carbon figure all draw a blank — that's the gap the customer pressure is really about. Source and Cycle had signals that sounded concerning, but neither showed an actual break in practice.
diagnosis.incorrectVerdict: Look again at Control: nobody can currently produce a device inventory, a disposal trail, or a CO₂ figure. Source and Cycle had signals that sounded concerning, but each one turned out to be a working practice, not a gap.

sections.title: Which step goes first?
sections.intro: This year the company will start exactly one main step. Constraints: tight budget, patchy data on old devices and emissions, a board that wants quick visible results, customers expecting traceable sustainability claims, and an IT team with limited capacity. Pick a first priority — you're not being graded, you're rehearsing the trade-off.
sections.tradeoffRelation: Judge the options on two different axes: how visible each is right now, versus how much it actually lets you steer for the long term. They're not the same thing — the fastest-looking move often steers the least.
sections.prompt: What should be the first main step this year?

options.label: A — Returns, refurbishment & reuse
options.summary: Stand up a proper return, refurbishment and reuse process for old devices.

consequence.headline: A direct, visible circular win — but it can't answer the CO₂ question yet.
points: Cuts waste immediately and gives a concrete story about responsible device handling.
Without a carbon baseline you still can't give the customer a traceable CO₂ figure.
Impact stays hard to prove and report, even while it's real.

options.label: B — Simplified IT carbon accounting
options.summary: Build a simplified IT carbon account: a baseline, pragmatic data sources, and clear ownership.

consequence.headline: Creates transparency and decision-ability — but must be paired with a device process.
points: Answers the reporting and customer-traceability demand head-on, at modest cost.
Improves management's ability to decide — you can finally steer, not just guess.
On its own it measures without yet reducing: pair it with a structured old-device process.

options.label: C — Replace devices with efficient models
options.summary: Swap old devices now for newer, more energy-efficient models.

consequence.headline: The fastest visible gesture — and the classic symbolic single step.
points: Looks green quickly, which pleases a board that wants something visible now.
New devices carry fresh embodied (grey) carbon; replacing early can raise the lifecycle total.
Scrapping still-usable hardware without a lifecycle review is what the coaching warns against.

sections.coachNote: The course's own reasoning leans toward B combined with a structured old-device process — transparency first, so every later step can be defended. But a well-argued choice under incomplete data is the real skill here; note what your pick commits you to next, and two risks if the first step turns out wrong.

sections.title: BlueGrid Solutions GmbH
sections.intro: A growing services firm, 1,100 staff, decentralised procurement across sites. Management wants — for the first time — a credible statement on IT's environmental impact. Read the starting position, then choose the first step you'd prioritise. You'll see it compared against the official recommendation.
situation: No central picture of the old-device inventory or where devices go next.
Disposal routes are not documented transparently or completely.
IT is worried about extra workload and complexity.
Management wants a solution that is both credible and practical.
levers: Build an IT-related carbon baseline from pragmatic data sources.
Set up an orderly return, reuse and refurbishment process for old devices.
Create clear ownership across IT, purchasing, sustainability and external partners.
Align procurement and replacement logic with lifecycle thinking.
sections.prompt: Which first step would you start with?

options.label: Simplified carbon baseline + structured old-device process, together
options.detail: Building a simplified carbon account alongside a structured old-device process creates transparency and credibility at once, and unites reporting, customer demand and operational improvement.
reasons: Improves management's ability to make decisions.
Unites reporting, customer demands and operational improvement.
Reduces the risk of a symbolic single step with no steering effect.

options.label: A big symbolic device refresh, to show customers something now
options.detail: A refresh is the photo-op trap: outwardly impressive, but with no baseline and no lifecycle review it improves neither steering nor credibility — and adds fresh embodied carbon.
reasons: No baseline means you still can't prove impact.
Adds embodied carbon while scrapping usable devices.
Impresses outwardly while changing little inside.

options.label: Publish a sustainability statement first, tighten the data later
options.detail: Claiming before you can trace invites exactly the audit questions BlueGrid can't yet answer. Transparency has to precede the statement, not follow it.
reasons: Unbacked claims fail under customer or audit scrutiny.
Erodes the credibility the exercise is meant to build.
Puts messaging ahead of the ability to steer.

options.label: Hand the whole topic to the external disposal vendor and wait
options.verdict: Outsources the governance, not just the work.
options.detail: A vendor can process devices, but ownership, data flows and the carbon baseline are management responsibilities that can't be delegated away.
reasons: Leaves no internal ownership or governance.
Still produces no IT carbon baseline.
Keeps disposal routes opaque rather than transparent.

sections.horizonsRelation: The two first moves — a baseline and a device process — are the foundation every later horizon builds on: short-term you gather data, medium-term you set rules, structurally you bake it into governance. Skip the foundation and the later steps have nothing to stand on.

horizons.label: Short-term
items: Inventory device types, replacement cycles and old-device flows.
Set a pragmatic IT CO₂ baseline.
Clarify internal authority and external process partners.

horizons.label: Medium-term
items: Record relevant emission and material data in a standardised way.

horizons.label: Structural
items: Embed carbon accounting and lifecycle management in IT governance and reporting.
Steer regularly through indicators, reviews and management decisions.

sections.title: Nexora Digital Services — your management proposal
sections.intro: You are the IT-governance lead / sustainability consultant for Nexora Digital Services: growing internationally, large device volumes, hybrid IT, mounting pressure to make the old-device inventory and CO₂ impact traceable — with no consistent steering model yet. This is a starter kit, not a form to fill in. Tick a component once you can argue it, and jot your line of reasoning. Everything saves on this device.
sections.seniorNote: Senior bar: don't produce a list of single actions — produce a robust decision architecture that ties together reporting, responsibility, lifecycle thinking and the ability to steer.
sections.architectureRelation: The seven parts aren't a checklist to tick off — they lock together into one structure: why it matters and what you report, who owns it and how data flows, the lifecycle it has to cover, and how you keep steering under uncertainty.

reflection.title: Reflection — carry these into the room
questions: Where does unnecessary e-waste arise in my organisation out of habit, not need?
Which decisions are currently taken with no CO₂ transparency?
Where would a visible step impress outsiders while being too weak inside?
Which decisions are robust long-term from the seat of a department head, architect or consultant?

glossary.title: Key terms
glossary.hint: Only the handful of terms this page actually uses.

terms.def: Retired electronic equipment — here, IT hardware and its components at end of use.
The energy already spent producing a device, before it is ever switched on. Kept by reuse, largely lost by early recycling.
Restoring a used device to reliable working order for continued use — higher on the ladder than recycling.
Rebuilding a device to as-new condition using recovered parts, more intensive than refurbishment.
Measuring an organisation's greenhouse-gas emissions so they can be reported and, above all, steered.
Direct emissions (1), purchased energy (2), and everything up- and downstream (3) — where most IT emissions sit.
A conversion rate turning an activity (kWh, a device, a shipment) into an estimated CO₂ figure.
What is counted and what is left out. Move the boundary and the reported number moves with it.
